claim: Axons contain exclusively 'plus-end-out' microtubules.
source: Conserved among both invertebrates and vertebrates, axons contain exclusively 'plus-end-out' microtubules while dendrites contain a high percentage of 'minus-end-out' microtubules, the origins of which have been a mystery.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work (Baas et al., 1988; Stepanova et al., 2003; Stone et al., 2008) as stated in the Introduction.

claim: Dendrites contain a high percentage of 'minus-end-out' microtubules.
source: Conserved among both invertebrates and vertebrates, axons contain exclusively 'plus-end-out' microtubules while dendrites contain a high percentage of 'minus-end-out' microtubules, the origins of which have been a mystery.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work (Baas et al., 1988; Stepanova et al., 2003; Stone et al., 2008) as stated in the Introduction.

claim: The dendritic growth cone contains a non-centrosomal microtubule organizing center (MTOC) in C. elegans.
source: Here we show that in Caenorhabditis elegans the dendritic growth cone contains a non-centrosomal microtubule organizing center (MTOC), which generates minus-end-out microtubules along outgrowing dendrites and plus-end-out microtubules in the growth cone.
evidence: This claim is supported by direct observations of EBP-2 comets and GIP-2 localization in the manuscript.

claim: The dendritic growth cone MTOC generates minus-end-out microtubules along outgrowing dendrites.
source: Here we show that in Caenorhabditis elegans the dendritic growth cone contains a non-centrosomal microtubule organizing center (MTOC), which generates minus-end-out microtubules along outgrowing dendrites and plus-end-out microtubules in the growth cone.
evidence: This is supported by EBP-2 comet tracking data showing minus-end-out MTs originating from the dgMTOC (Figure 1B and C).

claim: The dendritic growth cone MTOC generates plus-end-out microtubules in the growth cone.
source: Here we show that in Caenorhabditis elegans the dendritic growth cone contains a non-centrosomal microtubule organizing center (MTOC), which generates minus-end-out microtubules along outgrowing dendrites and plus-end-out microtubules in the growth cone.
evidence: This is supported by EBP-2 comet tracking data showing plus-end-out MTs in the distal growth cone region (Figure 1B and C).

claim: RAB-11-positive endosomes accumulate in the dendritic growth cone MTOC region.
source: RAB-11-positive endosomes accumulate in this region and co-migrate with the microtubule nucleation complex γ-TuRC.
evidence: This is supported by imaging data showing RAB-11.1 co-localization with GIP-2 (Figure 3D and E).

claim: RAB-11-positive endosomes co-migrate with the microtubule nucleation complex γ-TuRC.
source: RAB-11-positive endosomes accumulate in this region and co-migrate with the microtubule nucleation complex γ-TuRC.
evidence: This is supported by time-lapse imaging showing RAB-11.1 and GIP-2 moving together (Figure 3F and G).

claim: The MTOC tracks the extending growth cone by kinesin-1/UNC-116-mediated endosome movements on distal plus-end-out microtubules.
source: The MTOC tracks the extending growth cone by kinesin-1/UNC-116-mediated endosome movements on distal plus-end-out microtubules and dynein clusters this advancing MTOC.
evidence: This is supported by data showing GIP-2 movements are reduced in unc-116 mutants (Figure 4G-L) and that kinesin-1 is required for dgMTOC localization.

claim: Dynein clusters the advancing MTOC.
source: The MTOC tracks the extending growth cone by kinesin-1/UNC-116-mediated endosome movements on distal plus-end-out microtubules and dynein clusters this advancing MTOC.
evidence: This is supported by data showing GIP-2 dispersal in dhc-1 mutants (Figure 6E-K).

claim: Perturbation of the function or localization of the MTOC causes reversed microtubule polarity in dendrites.
source: Critically, perturbation of the function or localization of the MTOC causes reversed microtubule polarity in dendrites.
evidence: This is supported by data showing reversed MT polarity in GIP-1 knockdown (Figure 2F and G), unc-116 mutants (Figure 4A and B), and dhc-1 mutants (Figure 6N and O).

claim: The endosome-localized dendritic MTOC is critical for establishing axon-dendrite polarity.
source: These findings unveil the endosome-localized dendritic MTOC as a critical organelle for establishing axon-dendrite polarity.
evidence: This is supported by the observation that loss of the dgMTOC leads to reversed MT polarity in dendrites.

claim: In mature neurons, MTs are organized along the length of neurites with specific orientation.
source: For example, in mature neurons, MTs are organized along the length of neurites with specific orientation; axons contain exclusively plus-end-out MTs, while dendrites have predominantly minus-end-out or both plus-end-out and minus-end-out MTs in invertebrate and vertebrate species, respectively (Baas et al., 1988; Stepanova et al., 2003; Stone et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Dendrites with reversed MT orientation lose dendritic proteins and ectopically accumulate synaptic vesicles.
source: Dendrites with reversed MT orientation lose dendritic proteins and ectopically accumulate synaptic vesicles (Maniar et al., 2012; Yan et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: In cells, MT patterning is conferred by microtubule organizing centers (MTOCs).
source: In cells, MT patterning is conferred by microtubule organizing centers (MTOCs) (Pickett-Heaps, 1969), cellular sites which nucleate, anchor, and stabilize MT minus ends (Lüders and Stearns, 2007; Paz and Lüders, 2018; Sanchez and Feldman, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: During cell division, the centrosome acts as the MTOC to build the mitotic spindle.
source: During cell division, the centrosome acts as the MTOC to build the mitotic spindle.
evidence: This is established knowledge in cell biology.

claim: In many postmitotic differentiated cells such as neurons, centrosomes are inactive as MTOCs and often eliminated.
source: In many postmitotic differentiated cells such as neurons, centrosomes are inactive as MTOCs and often eliminated, and MTs instead associate with non-centrosomal sites such as the apical surface of epithelial cells and the nuclear envelope in skeletal muscle (Nguyen et al., 2011; Stiess et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Golgi outposts are frequently located at dendritic branch sites in mature Drosophila sensory neurons and can nucleate minus-end-out MTs.
source: In mature Drosophila sensory neurons, Golgi outposts are frequently located at dendritic branch sites and can nucleate minus-end-out MTs (Ori-McKenney et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Removal of Golgi outposts from dendrites does not alter minus-end-out MTs.
source: However, the role of Golgi outposts during development is unclear, and one study showed that removal of Golgi outposts from dendrites does not alter minus-end-out MTs (Nguyen et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: A subpopulation of early endosomes at branch sites house canonical Wnt signaling proteins and nucleate MTs to influence dendritic MT polarity after branching has occurred.
source: Furthermore, a recent study found that a subpopulation of early endosomes at branch sites house canonical Wnt signaling proteins and nucleate MTs to influence dendritic MT polarity after branching has occured (Weiner et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: In the dendrites of C. elegans ciliated neurons, microtubules are thought to be nucleated from the base of the cilium.
source: In the dendrites of C. elegans ciliated neurons, microtubules are thought to be nucleated from the base of the cilium, although this mechanism by definition is absent from non-ciliated neurons (Harterink et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: In rodent primary hippocampal cultures, short MTs could be delivered from the cell body to neurites by molecular motor-based sliding on other MTs.
source: In rodent primary hippocampal cultures, short MTs could be delivered from the cell body to neurites by molecular motor-based sliding on other MTs (Rao and Baas, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Kinesin-1 is required for the minus-end-out MTs in the mature dendrite of a C. elegans motor neuron.
source: Indeed, kinesin-1, a plus-end-directed motor is required for the minus-end-out MTs in the mature dendrite of a C. elegans motor neuron (Yan et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Kinesin-2 is required for minus-end-out MTs in Drosophila sensory dendrites through a mechanism of steering growing MT plus ends along pre-existing MTs.
source: Additionally, kinesin-2 is required for minus-end-out MTs in Drosophila sensory dendrites, although through an alternate proposed mechanism of steering growing MT plus ends along pre-existing MTs (Weiner et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: MT minus ends can grow in distal dendrites to form a uniformly minus-end-out MT array in branched Drosophila sensory dendrites.
source: Surprisingly, MT minus ends themselves can grow in distal dendrites to form a uniformly minus-end-out MT array in branched Drosophila sensory dendrites.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work (Feng et al., 2019).

claim: Loss of the MT minus end stabilizing protein Patronin reduces minus-end-out MTs in terminal dendrite branches.
source: Loss of the MT minus end stabilizing protein Patronin reduces minus-end-out MTs in terminal dendrite branches, while Patronin overexpression increases the percentage of minus-end-out MTs (Feng et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The primary anterior dendrite of PVD contains predominantly minus-end-out MTs.
source: The primary anterior dendrite of PVD contains predominantly minus-end-out MTs (Taylor et al., 2015), and we found that dendritic MTs were organized by a striking MTOC localized to the dendritic growth cone.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work and data in the manuscript.

claim: Numerous EBP-2 comets emerged from a single region within the distal neurite, suggesting the presence of a dendritic growth cone MTOC.
source: To investigate the establishment of minus-end-out MTs during dendrite outgrowth (step III in Figure 1A), we visualized the endogenous localization of the MT plus-end tracking protein EBP-2::GFP/EB1 in developing PVD anterior dendrites and found that numerous EBP-2 comets emerged from a single region within the distal neurite, suggesting the presence of a dendritic growth cone MTOC (dgMTOC, Figure 1B and Video 1).
evidence: This is supported by direct observation of EBP-2 dynamics in Figure 1B.

claim: Near the most distal region of the dendrite (~3–6 µm from the dendrite tip), almost all the EBP-2 comets move toward the distal tip indicating plus-end-out microtubules.
source: Near the most distal region of the dendrite (~3–6 µm from the dendrite tip), almost all the EBP-2 comets move toward the distal tip indicating plus-end-out microtubules, while nearly all the comets along the shaft of the anterior dendrite move toward the cell body indicating only minus-end-out MTs in this region (Figure 1B and C).
evidence: This is supported by quantification of EBP-2 comet direction in Figure 1C.

claim: Nearly all the comets along the shaft of the anterior dendrite move toward the cell body indicating only minus-end-out MTs in this region.
source: Near the most distal region of the dendrite (~3–6 µm from the dendrite tip), almost all the EBP-2 comets move toward the distal tip indicating plus-end-out microtubules, while nearly all the comets along the shaft of the anterior dendrite move toward the cell body indicating only minus-end-out MTs in this region (Figure 1B and C).
evidence: This is supported by quantification of EBP-2 comet direction in Figure 1C.

claim: The emergence of a high frequency of EBP-2 comets from a discrete region near the dendrite tip is consistent with the presence of a local MTOC.
source: The emergence of a high frequency of EBP-2 comets from a discrete region near the dendrite tip (mean = 0.44 comets/s±0.11 (SD) in a 3.2 µm region), which also encompasses a transition zone of MT directionality, is consistent with the presence of a local MTOC (Figure 1B and C).
evidence: This is supported by quantification of EBP-2 comet frequency in Figure 1B and C.

claim: This MT organization is apparent as soon as a morphologically distinct growth cone-tipped anterior dendrite has outgrown from the cell body and remains throughout the outgrowth of the anterior dendrite.
source: This MT organization is apparent as soon as a morphologically distinct growth cone-tipped anterior dendrite has outgrown from the cell body and remains throughout the outgrowth of the anterior dendrite (data not shown).
evidence: This is based on observations during imaging.

claim: The number of comets generated near the dendrite tip greatly exceeds comets from any other discrete point or region in the dendrite or from the cell body throughout the morphogenesis of the anterior dendrite.
source: In addition, the number of comets generated near the dendrite tip greatly exceeds comets from any other discrete point or region in the dendrite or from the cell body throughout the morphogenesis of the anterior dendrite, indicating that the dgMTOC is the only apparent MTOC.
evidence: This is based on quantification of EBP-2 comets.

claim: The axon and posterior dendrite, which contain predominantly plus-end-out MTs, do not contain similar structures to the dgMTOC.
source: The axon and posterior dendrite, which contain predominantly plus-end-out MTs, do not contain similar structures (Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data in Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: There is evidence for a similar dgMTOC near the tip of outgrowing Drosophila melanogaster Class I sensory vpda primary dendrites.
source: Significantly, we find evidence for a similar dgMTOC near the tip of outgrowing Drosophila melanogaster Class I sensory vpda primary dendrites (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D and Video 2), suggesting a conserved mechanism for the genesis of minus-end-out MTs in the primary dendrite.
evidence: This is supported by imaging data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D and Video 2.

claim: The dgMTOC suggests a conserved mechanism for the genesis of minus-end-out MTs in the primary dendrite.
source: Significantly, we find evidence for a similar dgMTOC near the tip of outgrowing Drosophila melanogaster Class I sensory vpda primary dendrites (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D and Video 2), suggesting a conserved mechanism for the genesis of minus-end-out MTs in the primary dendrite.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of similar structures in both C. elegans and Drosophila.

claim: TBA-1 was enriched in a region immediately behind the growth cone, consistent with the presence of a MTOC.
source: TBA-1 was enriched in a region immediately behind the growth cone (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E and F, Figure 1—source data 1), consistent with the presence of a MTOC.
evidence: This is supported by imaging data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E and F.

claim: Plus-end-out MTs extended distally toward the dendritic tip and minus-end-out MTs extended proximally toward the cell body from the dgMTOC.
source: This analysis also revealed an apparent dgMTOC from which plus-end-out MTs extended distally toward the dendritic tip and minus-end-out MTs extended proximally toward the cell body (blue and red lines, respectively, in Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by TBA-1 dynamics in Figure 1D.

claim: Numerous polymerization events originating from the dgMTOC were directed toward the cell body.
source: Consistent with the direction of EBP-2 comets, we observed numerous polymerization events originating from the dgMTOC and directed toward the cell body (red lines in Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by TBA-1 dynamics in Figure 1D.

claim: A similar frequency of depolymerization events was observed in the dgMTOC region, indicating that the majority of dgMTOC-derived minus-end-out MTs are highly dynamic.
source: A similar frequency of depolymerization events was also observed in this region (green lines in Figure 1D and Figure 1E, Figure 1—source data 1), indicating that the majority of dgMTOC-derived minus-end-out MTs are highly dynamic.
evidence: This is supported by quantification in Figure 1E.

claim: Both EBP-2 and TBA-1 dynamics suggest an active MTOC localizes to the dendritic growth cone region.
source: In summary, both EBP-2 and TBA-1 dynamics suggest an active MTOC localizes to the dendritic growth cone region.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined data of EBP-2 and TBA-1 dynamics.

claim: Microtubules are nucleated by the conserved γ-tubulin ring complex (γ-TuRC).
source: Microtubules are nucleated by the conserved γ-tubulin ring complex (γ-TuRC), a ring of γ-tubulin complex proteins (GCPs) that templates the assembly of new MTs (Oakley et al., 1990; Zheng et al., 1995).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: γ-TuRCs localize to MTOCs, including the centrosome.
source: γ-TuRCs localize to MTOCs, including the centrosome, the best studied MTOC which generates MTs from within its pericentriolar material (PCM) in dividing animal cells to form the mitotic spindle (Conduit et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: GIP-1 and GIP-2 consistently localized near the dendrite tip in a cluster of punctate structures which track with the growth cone in the outgrowing anterior dendrite.
source: We found that GIP-1 and GIP-2 consistently localized near the dendrite tip in a cluster of punctate structures which track with the growth cone in the outgrowing anterior dendrite (Figure 2A and B).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data in Figure 2A and B.

claim: GIP-1 precisely localized to the site from which EBP-2 comets originated.
source: GIP-1 precisely localized to the site from which EBP-2 comets originated (Figure 2C) and quantification of the distribution and location of GIP-1 and GIP-2 clusters showed that their location closely match the dgMTOC regions defined by EBP-2 comets (Figure 2D and E, Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data in Figure 2C.

claim: The location of GIP-1 and GIP-2 clusters closely match the dgMTOC regions defined by EBP-2 comets.
source: GIP-1 precisely localized to the site from which EBP-2 comets originated (Figure 2C) and quantification of the distribution and location of GIP-1 and GIP-2 clusters showed that their location closely match the dgMTOC regions defined by EBP-2 comets (Figure 2D and E, Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by quantification in Figure 2D and E.

claim: No GIP-1 or GIP-2 clusters were found in the cell body, axon, or posterior dendrite during their outgrowth.
source: These γ-TuRC clusters are specific to the outgrowing anterior dendrite since no GIP-1 or GIP-2 clusters were found in the cell body, axon, or posterior dendrite during their outgrowth (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and B), consistent with the lack of an apparent MTOC in these structures.
evidence: This is supported by imaging data in Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: Growth cone-localized GIP-2 was visible as soon as the anterior dendrite emerged but absent near the tip of mature dendrites.
source: Furthermore, growth cone-localized GIP-2 was visible as soon as the anterior dendrite emerged (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C) but absent near the tip of mature dendrites (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D), suggesting that the dgMTOC plays a role in the establishment of MT organization during dendrite development.
evidence: This is supported by imaging data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C and D.

claim: The dgMTOC plays a role in the establishment of MT organization during dendrite development.
source: Furthermore, growth cone-localized GIP-2 was visible as soon as the anterior dendrite emerged (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C) but absent near the tip of mature dendrites (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D), suggesting that the dgMTOC plays a role in the establishment of MT organization during dendrite development.
evidence: This is inferred from the temporal localization of GIP-2.

claim: GIP-2 localized close to the dendrite tip during dendrite outgrowth in the C. elegans DA9 motor neuron.
source: Significantly, GIP-2 also localized close to the dendrite tip during dendrite outgrowth in the C. elegans DA9 motor neuron (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E), further supporting a more general role for the dgMTOC in establishing dendritic minus-end-out MTs.
evidence: This is supported by imaging data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1E.

claim: The dgMTOC has a more general role in establishing dendritic minus-end-out MTs.
source: Significantly, GIP-2 also localized close to the dendrite tip during dendrite outgrowth in the C. elegans DA9 motor neuron (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E), further supporting a more general role for the dgMTOC in establishing dendritic minus-end-out MTs.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of GIP-2 localization in multiple neuron types.

claim: Expression of ZIF-1 in the developing PVD lineage led to a dramatic reduction of punctate GFP::GIP-1 signal in ~80% of outgrowing PVD anterior dendrites.
source: Expression of ZIF-1 in the developing PVD lineage led to a dramatic reduction of punctate GFP::GIP-1 signal in ~80% of outgrowing PVD anterior dendrites (GIP-1PVD(-), Figure 2—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1F.

claim: GIP-1PVD(-) animals showed a striking reversal of anterior dendrite MT polarity leading to plus-end-out orientation in both outgrowing and mature dendrites in about half of the animals.
source: We then examined EBP-2 comets in GIP-1PVD(-) animals, which revealed a striking reversal of anterior dendrite MT polarity leading to plus-end-out orientation in both outgrowing and mature dendrites in about half of the animals (Figure 2F and G, Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by quantification in Figure 2F and G.

claim: In GIP-1PVD(-) animals, many dendritic comets originated from the cell body.
source: Unlike in wild-type (wt) animals where the majority of EBP-2 comets were generated by the dgMTOC, in GIP-1PVD(-) animals, many dendritic comets originated from the cell body (Figure 2F and Video 3).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data in Figure 2F and Video 3.

claim: γ-TuRC is a critical component of the dgMTOC.
source: These results indicate that γ-TuRC is a critical component of the dgMTOC and that the dgMTOC is essential for establishing minus-end-out MTs in developing and mature dendrites.
evidence: This is inferred from the MT polarity defects observed upon GIP-1 depletion.

claim: The dgMTOC is essential for establishing minus-end-out MTs in developing and mature dendrites.
source: These results indicate that γ-TuRC is a critical component of the dgMTOC and that the dgMTOC is essential for establishing minus-end-out MTs in developing and mature dendrites.
evidence: This is inferred from the MT polarity defects observed upon GIP-1 depletion.

claim: The highest MT density was found ~2–4 µm from the dendritic tip, consistent with the presence of an MTOC in this region.
source: In our EM series, numerous short, staggered MTs were observed with their ends unambiguously identified. Consistent with our EBP-2 and TBA-1, the highest MT density was found ~2–4 µm from the dendritic tip, consistent with the presence of an MTOC in this region (Figure 3A–C, Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by EM reconstruction data in Figure 3A–C.

claim: Serial EM reconstruction showed no evidence of a centriole or Golgi outpost in the dgMTOC area.
source: Serial EM reconstruction showed no evidence of a centriole or Golgi outpost in the dgMTOC area.
evidence: This is based on EM reconstruction data.

claim: Numerous clear- and dense-core vesicles were found in between the MT arrays in the dgMTOC area.
source: Instead, numerous clear- and dense-core vesicles were found in between the MT arrays (Figure 3A and B).
evidence: This is supported by EM data in Figure 3A and B.

claim: Clusters of clear-core vesicles were found in the region with the highest MT numbers suggesting that GIP-1 and GIP-2 might localize to these vesicles to function in the dgMTOC.
source: In particular, clusters of clear-core vesicles (Figure 3B, white) were found in the region with the highest MT numbers suggesting that GIP-1 and GIP-2 might localize to these vesicles to function in the dgMTOC.
evidence: This is inferred from the co-localization of vesicles and high MT density.

claim: The synaptic vesicle marker RAB-3 was not enriched in the dendritic growth cone region.
source: Synaptic vesicles are the most abundant clear-core vesicles in neurons; however, the synaptic vesicle marker RAB-3, which robustly localized to the axon (Maniar et al., 2012), was not enriched in the dendritic growth cone region (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The early/medial Golgi cisternae markers RER-1 and AMAN-2/alpha-mannosidase 2 were only present in the cell body but not in the growth cone.
source: Consistent with our EM results, the early/medial Golgi cisternae markers RER-1 (Sato et al., 2011) and AMAN-2/alpha-mannosidase 2, the latter of which localizes to Golgi outpost MTOCs at mature dendrite branch sites in D. melanogaster (Ori-McKenney et al., 2012), were only present in the cell body but not in the growth cone (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B and C).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B and C.

claim: The late-Golgi compartment marker RAB-6.2 was enriched in the growth cone in a localization pattern similar to that of γ-TuRC.
source: Surprisingly, the late-Golgi compartment marker RAB-6.2 (Zhang et al., 2012) was enriched in the growth cone in a localization pattern similar to that of γ-TuRC (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B and C).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B and C.

claim: The recycling endosome marker RAB-11.1 co-localized and moved together with RAB-6.2-labeled vesicles in the growth cone.
source: Therefore, we further examined recycling endosomes and found that the recycling endosome marker RAB-11.1 co-localized and moved together with RAB-6.2-labeled vesicles in the growth cone (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D and E).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D and E.

claim: RAB-11.1 showed striking co-localization with GIP-2.
source: Notably, RAB-11.1 showed striking co-localization with GIP-2 (Figure 3D), with 81.7 ± 3.5% (SEM, n = 11) of RAB-11.1 fluorescence overlapping with GIP-2 and 80.6 ± 5.2% (SEM, n = 11) reciprocal GIP-2 fluorescence overlapping with RAB-11.1 in the growth cone (Figure 3E, Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by quantification in Figure 3D and E.

claim: RAB-11.1 displayed a nearly identical movement pattern to that of GIP-2, with both proteins moving together in the growth cone.
source: Time-lapse recordings revealed that RAB-11.1 displayed a nearly identical movement pattern to that of GIP-2, with both proteins moving together in the growth cone (Figure 3F and G).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data in Figure 3F and G.

claim: A frame-to-frame analysis of RAB-11.1 and GIP-2 distribution showed high correlation in the growth cone.
source: A frame-to-frame analysis of RAB-11.1 and GIP-2 distribution showed high correlation in the growth cone (Figure 3—figure supplement 1F), but no correlation in the cell body (Figure 3—figure supplement 1G; Costes et al., 2004; Manders et al., 1993).
evidence: This is supported by quantification in Figure 3—figure supplement 1F and G.

claim: Co-localization and co-trafficking of RAB11.1 and GIP-2 suggest that Rab11-endosomes may be at the core of the dgMTOC.
source: Co-localization and co-trafficking of RAB11.1 and GIP-2 suggest that Rab11-endosomes may be at the core of the dgMTOC.
evidence: This is inferred from the co-localization and co-trafficking data.

claim: Rab11-associated endosomes and Rab11 itself have been found to influence the MT organization of mitotic spindles.
source: Interestingly, Rab11-associated endosomes and even Rab11 itself have been found to influence the MT organization of mitotic spindles (Hehnly and Doxsey, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Expression of a dominant negative RAB-11.1(S25N) caused a loss of GIP-2 puncta from the dendritic growth cone in ~35% of animals.
source: Expression of a dominant negative RAB-11.1(S25N) (Ren et al., 1998) caused a loss of GIP-2 puncta from the dendritic growth cone in ~35% of animals (Figure 3H and J, n = 28, Figure 3—source data 1) and a reversed or mixed MT polarity in ~10% of animals (Figure 3—figure supplement 1H, n = 28).
evidence: This is supported by quantification in Figure 3H and J.

claim: Expression of a dominant negative RAB-11.1(S25N) caused a reversed or mixed MT polarity in ~10% of animals.
source: Expression of a dominant negative RAB-11.1(S25N) (Ren et al., 1998) caused a loss of GIP-2 puncta from the dendritic growth cone in ~35% of animals (Figure 3H and J, n = 28, Figure 3—source data 1) and a reversed or mixed MT polarity in ~10% of animals (Figure 3—figure supplement 1H, n = 28).
evidence: This is supported by quantification in Figure 3—figure supplement 1H.

claim: 20% of Cre expressing worms displayed a loss of GIP-2 puncta in the dendritic growth cone with mislocalization of GIP-2 as either multiple dim puncta dispersed within the cell body (12%) or along the dendrite shaft (7%).
source: 20% of Cre expressing worms displayed a loss of GIP-2 puncta in the dendritic growth cone with mislocalization of GIP-2 as either multiple dim puncta dispersed within the cell body (12%, Figure 3J,i1 and i2 in Figure 3I, n = 41) or along the dendrite shaft (7%, i3 in Figure 3I), suggesting transportation or clustering defects.
evidence: This is supported by quantification in Figure 3J and imaging in Figure 3I.

claim: γ-TuRC localization to RAB-11.1-positive endosomes in the growth cone underlies the dgMTOC, which generates short plus-end-out MTs in the distal growth cone and dynamic minus-end-out MTs that populate the growing dendrite.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that γ-TuRC localization to RAB-11.1-positive endosomes in the growth cone underlies the dgMTOC, which generates short plus-end-out MTs in the distal growth cone and dynamic minus-end-out MTs that populate the growing dendrite.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined data on γ-TuRC and RAB-11.1 localization and function.

claim: The mature PVD anterior dendrite loses minus-end-out MTs and gains plus-end-out MTs in unc-116/kinesin-1 mutants.
source: We previously showed that the mature PVD anterior dendrite loses minus-end-out MTs and gains plus-end-out MTs in unc-116/kinesin-1 mutants (Taylor et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: unc-116(e2310) mutants showed a large decrease in the percentage of minus-end-out MTs in the anterior dendrite shaft during outgrowth.
source: Consistent with the MT polarity defect in mature PVD dendrites, unc-116(e2310) mutants showed a large decrease in the percentage of minus-end-out MTs in the anterior dendrite shaft during outgrowth (wt: 93.8 ± 2.7% (SEM, n = 11); unc-116(e2310): 21.4 ± 10.4% (SEM, n = 12); Figure 4A and B, Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by quantification in Figure 4A and B.

claim: The reduced minus-end-out frequency in unc-116 mutants was partially rescued by expressing a wt unc-116(+) transgene during early neurite outgrowth.
source: Additionally, the reduced minus-end-out frequency in unc-116 mutants was partially rescued by expressing a wt unc-116(+) transgene during early neurite outgrowth (using the unc-86 promoter), but not rescued by expressing unc-116(+) after anterior dendrite outgrowth (using a ser-2 promoter), suggesting that UNC-116/Kinesin-1 is required specifically during early neurite outgrowth to establish dendritic minus-end-out MTs (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A, Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by quantification in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: UNC-116/Kinesin-1 is required specifically during early neurite outgrowth to establish dendritic minus-end-out MTs.
source: Additionally, the reduced minus-end-out frequency in unc-116 mutants was partially rescued by expressing a wt unc-116(+) transgene during early neurite outgrowth (using the unc-86 promoter), but not rescued by expressing unc-116(+) after anterior dendrite outgrowth (using a ser-2 promoter), suggesting that UNC-116/Kinesin-1 is required specifically during early neurite outgrowth to establish dendritic minus-end-out MTs (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A, Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: This is inferred from the rescue experiments.

claim: In unc-116 mutants, the vast majority of MTs originated from the cell body and were plus-end-out throughout the anterior dendrite.
source: In striking contrast to wt, unc-116 mutants lacked a convergence of plus-end-out and minus-end-out MTs in the outgrowing dendritic growth cone. Instead, the vast majority of MTs originated from the cell body and were plus-end-out throughout the anterior dendrite (Figure 4A, Figure 4—figure supplement 1C and D and Video 4), raising the possibility that the dgMTOC is inactive or mislocalized in unc-116 mutants.
evidence: This is supported by imaging data in Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1C and D.

claim: In unc-116 mutants, many EBP-2 comets emanated from a single region within the cell body indicating a putative MTOC.
source: By tracing the origin of EBP-2 comets over time in unc-116 mutants, we frequently observed that many EBP-2 comets emanated from a single region within the cell body indicating a putative MTOC (Figure 4C and Video 5) – a stark contrast to the lack of a point-of-origin for EBP-2 comets in GIP-1PVD(-) animals (Video 3).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data in Figure 4C and Video 5.

claim: GIP-2 was largely absent from the outgrowing dendritic growth cone and instead formed a cluster within the cell body in 64% of unc-116 mutants.
source: Unlike in wt, GIP-2 was largely absent from the outgrowing dendritic growth cone and instead formed a cluster within the cell body in 64% of unc-116 mutants (n = 45, Figure 4D and Figure 4—figure supplement 1E, Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by quantification in Figure 4D and Figure 4—figure supplement 1E.

claim: RAB-11.1 formed a cluster within the cell body rather than in the growth cone region in 71% of unc-116 mutants.
source: RAB-11.1 also formed a cluster within the cell body rather than in the growth cone region in 71% of unc-116 mutants (n = 28, Figure 4E and Figure 4—figure supplement 1F, Figure 4—source data 1), providing further support that Rab11 endosomes are a component of the dgMTOC.
evidence: This is supported by quantification in Figure 4E and Figure 4—figure supplement 1F.

claim: The kinesin-1 motor is required for localizing the dgMTOC to the outgrowing dendritic growth cone.
source: Together, these results indicate that the kinesin-1 motor is required for localizing the dgMTOC to the outgrowing dendritic growth cone.
evidence: This is inferred from the mislocalization of the dgMTOC in unc-116 mutants.

claim: The location of the dgMTOC instructs MT polarity.
source: Furthermore, while depletion of GIP-1 in PVD showed that the dgMTOC is required to establish dendritic minus-end-out MTs, this unc-116 mutant phenotype suggests that the location of the dgMTOC instructs MT polarity.
evidence: This is inferred from the correlation between dgMTOC location and MT polarity.

claim: GIP-2 fluorescence undergoes processive movements toward the distal tip.
source: Time-lapse analyses of GIP-2 cluster movement showed that GIP-2 fluorescence undergoes processive movements toward the distal tip with several features.
evidence: This is supported by time-lapse imaging data in Figure 4F.

claim: GIP-2 movements are largely unidirectional toward the distal dendrite tip.
source: First, GIP-2 movements are largely unidirectional toward the distal dendrite tip, which is evident in kymograph analysis (f1 in Figure 4F), GIP-2 cluster localization at different time points (left and right panels of f2 in Figure 4F) and quantification of the anterior displacement of the GIP-2 cluster (Figure 4K).
evidence: This is supported by quantification in Figure 4K.

claim: GIP-2 localization alternates between a tight cluster and a broader cluster with more dispersed puncta.
source: Second, GIP-2 localization alternates between a tight cluster and a broader cluster with more dispersed puncta (middle and right panels of f2 in Figure 4F).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data in Figure 4F.

claim: GIP-2 movements are interspersed by pauses.
source: Third, the movements are interspersed by pauses (middle panel of f2 in Figure 4F), which is also evident by the alternating slopes and plateaus in GIP-2 moving distance analyses (black trace in Figure 4I and Figure 4—figure supplement 2A, Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by quantification in Figure 4I and Figure 4—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Most GIP-2 exists in a bright cluster during pauses, while the fluorescence is dispersed into multiple smaller puncta during the mobile phase.
source: Most GIP-2 exists in a bright cluster during pauses, while the fluorescence is dispersed into multiple smaller puncta during the mobile phase (f2 in Figure 4F and Video 6).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data in Figure 4F and Video 6.

claim: GIP-2 moves in a saltatory manner, with cycles of aggregation and dispersal, toward the distal dendritic tip.
source: These results indicate that GIP-2 moves in a saltatory manner, with cycles of aggregation and dispersal, toward the distal dendritic tip.
evidence: This is inferred from the observed dynamics of GIP-2 movement.

claim: unc-116/kinesin-1 mutants showed largely reduced movement or dispersal of GIP-2 clusters.
source: Consistent with this idea, unc-116/kinesin-1 mutants showed largely reduced movement or dispersal of GIP-2 clusters (Figure 4G and J–L, Figure 4—figure supplement 2B and Video 7, Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by quantification in Figure 4G and J–L.

claim: UNC-116/kinesin-1 moves GIP-2 containing endosomes in the outgrowing dendrite.
source: These analyses suggest that UNC-116/kinesin-1 moves GIP-2 containing endosomes in the outgrowing dendrite.
evidence: This is inferred from the reduced GIP-2 movement in unc-116 mutants.

claim: The individual plus-end-out MTs displayed frequent pauses between polymerization and depolymerization that lasted 10.34 ± 0.85 s (SEM, n = 34).
source: Interestingly, we noticed that unlike minus-end-out MTs which transitioned rapidly between polymerization and depolymerization (Figures 1C and D and a3 in Figure 5A, triangle-shaped peaks in kymographs, Figure 5—source data 1), the individual plus-end-out MTs displayed frequent pauses between polymerization and depolymerization that lasted 10.34 ± 0.85 s (SEM, n = 34) (a2 in Figure 5A, plateaus, Figure 5B and C, Figure 5—source data 1), indicating that the distal plus-end-out MTs are transiently stabilized, likely through interaction with the growth cone.
evidence: This is supported by quantification in Figure 5B and C.

claim: The distal plus-end-out MTs are transiently stabilized, likely through interaction with the growth cone.
source: Interestingly, we noticed that unlike minus-end-out MTs which transitioned rapidly between polymerization and depolymerization (Figures 1C and D and a3 in Figure 5A, triangle-shaped peaks in kymographs, Figure 5—source data 1), the individual plus-end-out MTs displayed frequent pauses between polymerization and depolymerization that lasted 10.34 ± 0.85 s (SEM, n = 34) (a2 in Figure 5A, plateaus, Figure 5B and C, Figure 5—source data 1), indicating that the distal plus-end-out MTs are transiently stabilized, likely through interaction with the growth cone.
evidence: This is inferred from the observed pausing behavior of plus-end-out MTs.

claim: The distal plus-end-out MTs originating from the cell body in unc-116 mutants also paused in the tip of the dendrite and showed similar pause frequency and time as wt animals.
source: We note that the distal plus-end-out MTs originating from the cell body in unc-116 mutants also paused in the tip of the dendrite and showed similar pause frequency and time as wt animals (Figure 5B and C, Figure 5—source data 1), indicating that the pausing of plus-end-out MTs in the growth cone is independent of UNC-116 function.
evidence: This is supported by quantification in Figure 5B and C.

claim: The pausing of plus-end-out MTs in the growth cone is independent of UNC-116 function.
source: We note that the distal plus-end-out MTs originating from the cell body in unc-116 mutants also paused in the tip of the dendrite and showed similar pause frequency and time as wt animals (Figure 5B and C, Figure 5—source data 1), indicating that the pausing of plus-end-out MTs in the growth cone is independent of UNC-116 function.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of MT pausing in wt and unc-116 mutants.

claim: Kinesin-1 has been shown to prefer transporting cargoes on stable over dynamic MTs.
source: Kinesin-1 has been shown to prefer transporting cargoes on stable over dynamic MTs (Cai et al., 2009; Konishi and Setou, 2009; Tas et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: No obvious distal directed RAB-11.1 movements were observed when only dynamic plus-end-out MTs were present.
source: No obvious distal directed RAB-11.1 movements were observed when only dynamic plus-end-out MTs were present (d1 in Figure 5D).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data in Figure 5D.

claim: Endosome movements toward the distal dendritic tip were observed in the presence of stable plus-end-out MTs.
source: In contrast, endosome movements toward the distal dendritic tip were observed in the presence of stable plus-end-out MTs (d2 in Figure 5D, orange lines).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data in Figure 5D.

claim: Endosome movements preferentially occurred during periods with paused MTs.
source: We found that endosome movements preferentially occurred during periods with paused MTs (red portion of solid line in Figure 5E and red portion of Figure 5—figure supplement 1A) and there was no obvious RAB-11.1 movement when the plus-end-out MTs were dynamic (dashed line in Figure 5E and black portion in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A, Figure 5—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by quantification in Figure 5E and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: RAB-11.1 endosome moving distance showed a positive correlation with the total MT pause time overall.
source: By sampling of a population of worms, we found that RAB-11.1 endosome moving distance showed a positive correlation with the total MT pause time overall (Figure 5F, Figure 5—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by quantification in Figure 5F.

claim: Distally-directed endosomes move on paused or stable plus-end-out MTs in a kinesin-1-dependent manner.
source: These results suggest that distally-directed endosomes move on paused or stable plus-end-out MTs in a kinesin-1-dependent manner.
evidence: This is inferred from the correlation between endosome movement and MT pausing.

claim: Kinesin-1 transports γ-TuRC-positive endosomes toward the dendritic tip as the growth cone advances.
source: Taken together, these findings are consistent with a model in which kinesin-1 transports γ-TuRC-positive endosomes toward the dendritic tip as the growth cone advances.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined data on kinesin-1 function and endosome movement.

claim: The γ-TuRC at the dgMTOC builds plus-end-out MTs toward the growth cone, which serve as tracks for the next bouts of kinesin-1-mediated endosome movements.
source: The γ-TuRC at the dgMTOC builds plus-end-out MTs toward the growth cone, which serve as tracks for the next bouts of kinesin-1-mediated endosome movements.
evidence: This is inferred from the observed dynamics of MT nucleation and endosome movement.

claim: Cytoplasmic dynein has been shown to concentrate organelles such as Golgi or Rab11 endosomes near MTOCs in non-neuronal cells.
source: Cytoplasmic dynein has been shown to concentrate organelles such as Golgi or Rab11 endosomes near MTOCs in non-neuronal cells (Corthésy-Theulaz et al., 1992; Horgan et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: In ~30% of dhc-1 mutants, GIP-2 clusters were completely absent from the PVD anterior dendrite and the rest of the cell.
source: dhc-1(or195), a temperature-sensitive dynein mutant, displayed several types of defects in dgMTOC localization when animals were cultured at the nonpermissive temperature. In ~30% of dhc-1 mutants, GIP-2 clusters were completely absent from the PVD anterior dendrite and the rest of the cell (compare wt localization in Figure 6A to b1 in Figure 6B, Figure 6C, Figure 6—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by quantification in Figure 6C.

claim: In ~40% of dhc-1 mutant animals, one or several GIP-2 cluster(s) could be found in the cell body and occasionally in the posterior dendrite.
source: In another ~40% of mutant animals, one or several GIP-2 cluster(s) could be found in the cell body and occasionally in the posterior dendrite (b2 in Figure 6B, Figure 6C).
evidence: This is supported by quantification in Figure 6C.

claim: In ~30% of dhc-1 mutant animals, a GIP-2 cluster still localized to the anterior dendrite but showed a variable distance to the dendritic tip which was longer than in wt animals.
source: In the remaining ~30% of mutant animals, a GIP-2 cluster still localized to the anterior dendrite but showed a variable distance to the dendritic tip which was longer than in wt animals (b3 in Figure 6B, Figure 6C and D, Figure 6—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by quantification in Figure 6C and D.

claim: Net GIP-2 movement toward the dendritic tip was reduced in dhc-1 mutant worms compared to wt.
source: Time-lapse imaging analysis of GIP-2 movements in the subset of dhc-1 mutant worms which have an anterior dendrite-localized GIP-2 cluster showed that net GIP-2 movement toward the dendritic tip was reduced compared to that of wt, consistent with its ectopic localization.
evidence: This is supported by quantification in Figure 6I.

claim: GIP-2 puncta in dhc-1 mutants exhibited repeated dispersal and failed to form a relatively stable singular cluster.
source: Strikingly, further analyses of dhc-1 mutants showed that GIP-2 puncta exhibited repeated dispersal and failed to form a relatively stable singular cluster (Figure 6E–I, Figure 4—figure supplement 2C, Video 8 and Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data in Figure 6E–I and Video 8.

claim: The continuous dispersal of GIP-2 clusters led to a reduction in the maximal intensity of the cluster over time which might explain the lack of GIP-2 clusters in a subset of dhc-1 mutants.
source: The continuous dispersal of GIP-2 clusters led to a reduction in the maximal intensity of the cluster over time which might explain the lack of GIP-2 clusters in a subset of dhc-1 mutants (Figure 6J and K, Figure 6—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by quantification in Figure 6J and K.

claim: Endogenously tagged DHC-1 localized to the dgMTOC region as a cluster and remained associated with the base of the advancing growth cone.
source: Endogenously tagged DHC-1 localized to the dgMTOC region as a cluster and like the GIP-2 clusters remained associated with the base of the advancing growth cone (Figure 6L).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data in Figure 6L.

claim: DHC-1 dynamic movements closely coincided with those of RAB-11.1 foci.
source: These dynamic movements closely coincided with those of RAB-11.1 foci (Figure 6M).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data in Figure 6M.

claim: DHC-1 functions locally at the dgMTOC to move RAB-11.1 endosomes.
source: This striking subcellular localization of DHC-1 further suggests that DHC-1 functions locally at the dgMTOC to move RAB-11.1 endosomes.
evidence: This is inferred from the co-localization and co-movement of DHC-1 and RAB-11.1.

claim: About 50% of dhc-1 mutants showed complete reversal of MT polarity.
source: Consistent with the defect in dgMTOC localization, we found that about 50% of dhc-1 mutants showed complete reversal of MT polarity (n1 in Figure 6N) while another 20% of mutants showed mixed plus-end-out and minus-end-out MTs in the anterior dendrites (n2 in Figure 6N) perhaps due to the dispersed GIP-2 clusters in these mutants (Figure 6N and O, Figure 6—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by quantification in Figure 6N and O.

claim: About 20% of dhc-1 mutants showed mixed plus-end-out and minus-end-out MTs in the anterior dendrites.
source: Consistent with the defect in dgMTOC localization, we found that about 50% of dhc-1 mutants showed complete reversal of MT polarity (n1 in Figure 6N) while another 20% of mutants showed mixed plus-end-out and minus-end-out MTs in the anterior dendrites (n2 in Figure 6N) perhaps due to the dispersed GIP-2 clusters in these mutants (Figure 6N and O, Figure 6—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by quantification in Figure 6N and O.

claim: Dynein uses its minus-end-directed motor activity to re-cluster γ-TuRC-positive endosomes together which had dispersed during translocation towards the distal tip of the dendritic growth cone by kinesin-1.
source: These results suggest that dynein uses its minus-end-directed motor activity to re-cluster γ-TuRC-positive endosomes together which had dispersed during translocation towards the distal tip of the dendritic growth cone by kinesin-1, and this clustering is required for establishing dendritic minus-end-out MT polarity.
evidence: This is inferred from the dispersal of GIP-2 in dhc-1 mutants and the role of dynein as a minus-end-directed motor.

claim: Dynein clustering of γ-TuRC-positive endosomes is required for establishing dendritic minus-end-out MT polarity.
source: These results suggest that dynein uses its minus-end-directed motor activity to re-cluster γ-TuRC-positive endosomes together which had dispersed during translocation towards the distal tip of the dendritic growth cone by kinesin-1, and this clustering is required for establishing dendritic minus-end-out MT polarity.
evidence: This is inferred from the MT polarity defects in dhc-1 mutants.

claim: MTs in the dendrite are locally generated by a γ-TuRC-based endosome-associated dgMTOC which advances with the growing dendrite by the concerted action of both kinesin-1 and dynein.
source: Collectively, these data support a model in which MTs in the dendrite are locally generated by a γ-TuRC-based endosome-associated dgMTOC which advances with the growing dendrite by the concerted action of both kinesin-1 and dynein (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a summary of the findings presented in the manuscript.

claim: The mobile dgMTOC is required to establish the initial minus-end-out MT polarity during development that will be retained in the mature neuron for proper neuronal function.
source: Significantly, we found that the mobile dgMTOC is required to establish the initial minus-end-out MT polarity during development that will be retained in the mature neuron for proper neuronal function.
evidence: This is inferred from the MT polarity defects observed when the dgMTOC is disrupted.

claim: The conserved microtubule nucleating complex γ-TuRC localized to the dgMTOC and was necessary for minus-end-out MT polarity in the dendrite.
source: Consistently, the conserved microtubule nucleating complex γ-TuRC localized to the dgMTOC and was necessary for minus-end-out MT polarity in the dendrite.
evidence: This is supported by the localization of GIP-1 and GIP-2 to the dgMTOC and the MT polarity defects in GIP-1 knockdown.

claim: Mislocalization of the dgMTOC in both kinesin-1 and dynein mutants resulted in a lack of minus-end-out MTs in the dendrite.
source: Furthermore, mislocalization of the dgMTOC in both kinesin-1 and dynein mutants resulted in a lack of minus-end-out MTs in the dendrite.
evidence: This is supported by the MT polarity defects in unc-116 and dhc-1 mutants.

claim: The presence of the dgMTOC appears to be instructive for minus-end-out MTs since a small portion of kinesin-1 mutants mislocalized the dgMTOC to the posterior dendrite and had ectopic minus-end-out MTs in the posterior dendrite.
source: In fact, the presence of the dgMTOC appears to be instructive for minus-end-out MTs since a small portion of kinesin-1 mutants mislocalized the dgMTOC to the posterior dendrite and had ectopic minus-end-out MTs in the posterior dendrite.
evidence: This is supported by the observation of ectopic minus-end-out MTs in the posterior dendrite when the dgMTOC is mislocalized there.

claim: The minus-end-out orientation of dendritic MTs initially established by the dgMTOC is likely maintained by additional mechanisms.
source: The minus-end-out orientation of dendritic MTs initially established by the dgMTOC is likely maintained by additional mechanisms.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that the dgMTOC is absent in mature dendrites but minus-end-out MTs are maintained.

claim: Both EM reconstruction and TBA-1/α-tubulin dynamics in the primary dendrite show that minus-end-out MTs form a short-staggered array.
source: Both EM reconstruction and TBA-1/α-tubulin dynamics in the primary dendrite show that minus-end-out MTs form a short-staggered array, which suggests that MTs do not always remain associated with the dgMTOC during outgrowth.
evidence: This is supported by EM reconstruction data in Figure 3 and TBA-1 dynamics.

claim: Cortical anchoring of MTs through an Ankyrin-CRMP complex has been shown to immobilize MTs to regulate MT stability and polarity in mature dendrites.
source: Recently, cortical anchoring of MTs through an Ankyrin-CRMP complex has been showed to immobilize MTs to regulate MT stability and polarity in mature dendrites (He et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Minus-end-out MT polarity of the entire dendritic MT array is maintained throughout the entire lifetime of an organism.
source: Minus-end-out MT polarity of the entire dendritic MT array is maintained throughout the entire lifetime of an organism, which is likely achieved through a collaboration of multiple MT orientation-guiding mechanisms previously shown to act in later stages of development.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that minus-end-out MTs are maintained in mature dendrites.

claim: The minus end growth mediated by Patronin in Drosophila neurons grows minus-end-out MTs into terminal branches.
source: The minus end growth mediated by Patronin in Drosophila neurons grows minus-end-out MTs into terminal branches, which undergo a transition from a mixed polarity MTs to predominantly minus-end-out MTs as the dendrites mature.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work (Feng et al., 2019).

claim: Minus-end-out MTs still initially develop in the primary dendrites of patronin mutants.
source: However, minus-end-out MTs still initially develop in the primary dendrites of patronin mutants (Feng et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The dgMTOC is responsible for generating minus-end-out MTs in the primary dendrite of PVD as soon as the dendrite grows out before secondary branches elaborate.
source: In contrast, the dgMTOC is responsible for generating minus-end-out MTs in the primary dendrite of PVD as soon as the dendrite grows out before secondary branches elaborate.
evidence: This is supported by the observation of the dgMTOC during early dendrite outgrowth.

claim: At a later developmental stage when the dgMTOC is absent from PVD, MTs populate a portion of the secondary branches, likely through a dgMTOC-independent mechanism.
source: At a later developmental stage when the dgMTOC is absent from PVD, MTs populate a portion of the secondary branches, likely through a dgMTOC-independent mechanism (Liu et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: RAB-11.1 co-localized and co-trafficked with γ-TuRC at the site of the dgMTOC in the growth cone.
source: Importantly, our data demonstrate that the minus-end-out orientation of MTs in the dendrite – which is essential for their function in polarized trafficking – is established by a remarkably mobile endosome-associated MTOC. RAB-11.1 co-localized and co-trafficked with γ-TuRC at the site of the dgMTOC in the growth cone, and RAB-11.1 mis-localized to the same location as γ-TuRC and MTOC activity in unc-116/kinesin-1 mutants, consistent with the model that RAB-11.1-marked endosomes provide a scaffold onto which γ-TuRC assembles to form the dgMTOC.
evidence: This is supported by imaging data showing co-localization and co-trafficking of RAB-11.1 and GIP-2.

claim: RAB-11.1 mis-localized to the same location as γ-TuRC and MTOC activity in unc-116/kinesin-1 mutants.
source: Importantly, our data demonstrate that the minus-end-out orientation of MTs in the dendrite – which is essential for their function in polarized trafficking – is established by a remarkably mobile endosome-associated MTOC. RAB-11.1 co-localized and co-trafficked with γ-TuRC at the site of the dgMTOC in the growth cone, and RAB-11.1 mis-localized to the same location as γ-TuRC and MTOC activity in unc-116/kinesin-1 mutants, consistent with the model that RAB-11.1-marked endosomes provide a scaffold onto which γ-TuRC assembles to form the dgMTOC.
evidence: This is supported by imaging data showing RAB-11.1 localization in unc-116 mutants.

claim: RAB-11.1-marked endosomes provide a scaffold onto which γ-TuRC assembles to form the dgMTOC.
source: Importantly, our data demonstrate that the minus-end-out orientation of MTs in the dendrite – which is essential for their function in polarized trafficking – is established by a remarkably mobile endosome-associated MTOC. RAB-11.1 co-localized and co-trafficked with γ-TuRC at the site of the dgMTOC in the growth cone, and RAB-11.1 mis-localized to the same location as γ-TuRC and MTOC activity in unc-116/kinesin-1 mutants, consistent with the model that RAB-11.1-marked endosomes provide a scaffold onto which γ-TuRC assembles to form the dgMTOC.
evidence: This is inferred from the co-localization and co-trafficking data.

claim: Rab11-associated endosomes in mitotic cells can deliver spindle material to the centrosome.
source: Rab11-associated endosomes in mitotic cells can deliver spindle material to the centrosome, suggesting that Rab11-endosomes might be a general source of MTOC material (Hehnly and Doxsey, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Rab11-endosomes might be a general source of MTOC material.
source: Rab11-associated endosomes in mitotic cells can deliver spindle material to the centrosome, suggesting that Rab11-endosomes might be a general source of MTOC material (Hehnly and Doxsey, 2014).
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of Rab11-endosomes in mitotic cells.

claim: Interference with endogenous RAB-11.1 in PVD interfered with γ-TuRC localization to the dendritic growth cone.
source: Notably, interference with endogenous RAB-11.1 in PVD interfered with γ-TuRC localization to the dendritic growth cone, suggesting that RAB-11.1 itself may influence the dgMTOC.
evidence: This is supported by data showing GIP-2 mislocalization in RAB-11.1 knockdown.

claim: RAB-11.1 itself may influence the dgMTOC.
source: Notably, interference with endogenous RAB-11.1 in PVD interfered with γ-TuRC localization to the dendritic growth cone, suggesting that RAB-11.1 itself may influence the dgMTOC.
evidence: This is inferred from the effects of RAB-11.1 knockdown on GIP-2 localization.

claim: During mitosis, endosome transportation is regulated by the interaction between Rab11 and dynein.
source: During mitosis, endosome transportation is regulated by the interaction between Rab11 and dynein (Hehnly and Doxsey, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: RAB-11.1 may interact with dynein to localize and cluster the dgMTOC.
source: When we knocked out rab-11.1 in PVD, γ-TuRC was mislocalized as dispersed puncta, similar to the dynein mutant, consistent with the idea that RAB-11.1 may interact with dynein to localize and cluster the dgMTOC.
evidence: This is inferred from the similarity of phenotypes in RAB-11.1 knockdown and dynein mutants.

claim: The dgMTOC is a widespread phenomenon and a generally conserved mechanism for establishing a minus-end-out MT population in primary dendrites.
source: Finally, our data and that of others support the notion that the dgMTOC is a widespread phenomenon and a generally conserved mechanism for establishing a minus-end-out MT population in primary dendrites.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of dgMTOCs in multiple species and neuron types.

claim: Both anterograde and retrograde microtubule polymerization appear to originate from the same site in the dendritic growth cone of Drosophila sensory neurons.
source: In a recent study looking at cytoskeletal interplay during primary dendrite branching of Drosophila sensory neurons, both anterograde and retrograde microtubule polymerization appear to originate from the same site in the dendritic growth cone (Yoong et al., 2020), as we show here, indicating the presence of a dgMTOC.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Drosophila sensory neurons often have two primary dendrites both of which appear to have their own dgMTOCs.
source: Notably, these sensory neurons often have two primary dendrites both of which appear to have their own dgMTOCs, suggesting that multiple dgMTOCs can exist in different processes to establish minus-end-out MTs.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of dgMTOCs in multiple dendrites.

claim: Multiple dgMTOCs can exist in different processes to establish minus-end-out MTs.
source: Notably, these sensory neurons often have two primary dendrites both of which appear to have their own dgMTOCs, suggesting that multiple dgMTOCs can exist in different processes to establish minus-end-out MTs.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of dgMTOCs in multiple dendrites.

claim: In mammalian neurons, dendrites contain both plus-end-out and minus-end-out MTs.
source: In mammalian neurons, dendrites contain both plus-end-out and minus-end-out MTs.
evidence: This is established knowledge in neuroscience.

claim: A dgMTOC could establish the minus-end-out MT population during dendrite outgrowth in mammalian neurons.
source: We imagine a dgMTOC could establish the minus-end-out MT population during dendrite outgrowth in this system as well.
evidence: This is speculative based on the findings in C. elegans and Drosophila.

claim: Diverse cell types can tune other local and overall MT dynamics and maintenance programs to achieve different relative levels of plus-end-out and minus-end-out MTs to maintain a mixed polarity dendritic MT population.
source: We speculate that diverse cell types can tune other local and overall MT dynamics and maintenance programs to achieve different relative levels of plus-end-out and minus-end-out MTs to maintain a mixed polarity dendritic MT population.
evidence: This is speculative based on the findings in the manuscript.
